description: Per-event forced-liquidation history for Gate.io USDT perpetuals, backfilled hour by hour by scripts/fetch_gate_liquidations.py. This is the ONLY route measured that reaches back in time at event resolution: Gate serves a rolling ~90 days with no auth, OKX only ~24 hours, Coinalyze only 7 days and only as time-bucketed aggregates, and Binance and BitMEX publish no history at all (docs/DATA/surveys/LIQUIDATION_HISTORY_SURVEY.md). The window ROLLS, so anything not pulled is lost permanently -- that is why this is a snapshot under backtest_data/ rather than a live feed. Motivation: the owner's katsuo bot read long wicks as the fingerprint of a liquidation cascade running out of fuel; this dataset lets that mechanism be examined on past data instead of waiting for the live recorder to accumulate it (docs/STRATEGY_IDEAS.md O-3, O-3c, O-6).
source: GET https://api.gateio.ws/api/v4/futures/usdt/liq_orders?contract=<CONTRACT>&from=&to=&limit=1000 -- public, no auth, read only. API constraints measured 2026-09-08: the from/to range must be <= 1 hour, both ends are INCLUSIVE (from=to=T returns the rows at exactly T), limit caps at 1000, and passing only `to` implies a 1-hour window ending there. Hence the hour-by-hour walk.
retention: permanent snapshot. Gate's own window is rolling ~90 days, so the old end of this file cannot be re-fetched once it ages out. Re-running the script appends newer hours; it never rewrites existing lines.

contract.meaning: Gate contract the liquidation happened on
contract.notes: one file per contract; the field is kept anyway because the rows are stored exactly as returned

time.meaning: when the liquidation order was recorded by Gate
time.notes: second resolution only -- coarser than the live recorder's microsecond recv_us. Many rows share a second during a cascade, and their order within that second is not recoverable

size.notes: the sign carries the direction: negative = a long was liquidated (the forced order SELLS), positive = a short was liquidated (the forced order BUYS). This sign is the whole point for the katsuo mechanism -- do not take abs() without saying so

order_size.meaning: size of the forced order placed

left.meaning: unfilled remainder of the forced order
left.notes: 0 in every row observed on 2026-09-08; not verified to be always 0

fill_price.meaning: price the forced order actually filled at
fill_price.notes: string in the JSON, not a number

order_price.meaning: price the forced order was placed at (the bankruptcy/liquidation price)
order_price.notes: string in the JSON. order_price - fill_price is the slippage the liquidation engine ate, which is one direct measure of how much fuel the cascade consumed

known_defects: COVERAGE IS DEFINED BY THE SIDECAR, NOT THE DATA FILE. <CONTRACT>.progress.json lists every hour actually requested and how many rows it returned. An hour absent from that file was never fetched; an hour present with n=0 genuinely had no liquidations. Without consulting it, an empty stretch in the data cannot be told from a gap -- i.e. a negative cannot be told from an unknown.

rows carry no unique id, so identical tuples cannot be told apart. The fetcher avoids duplicates structurally instead: windows are [frm, frm+3599] stepping by 3600 with both ends inclusive, so they neither overlap nor leave gaps. A reader must NOT dedupe on the tuple -- two genuine liquidations in the same second with the same size and prices are indistinguishable and both are real.

a window that returns exactly 1000 rows is saturated and was silently truncated by the API. Saturation happens precisely during cascades -- the windows the katsuo mechanism most wants -- so the fetcher does not settle for a coarse retry: it halves the span and re-fetches recursively down to a single second. Only a span of one second that still returns 1000 rows is unrecoverable; those are listed in the manifest as hours_with_truncation, keyed by hour, with the exact [from, to] seconds. An empty hours_with_truncation means nothing was truncated. Never infer a rate from a window listed there.
timestamps are seconds, and no receive-time is recorded, so this dataset cannot measure observation delay the way data/liquidations/ can. Do not mix the two when timing anything at sub-second scale.
the current hour is never fetched (it is still filling), so the newest edge of the file lags up to two hours behind the run time.

the fetcher stops after 48 consecutive empty hours, treating that as the far edge of Gate's retention window. If Gate were genuinely quiet for two days on a contract, the walk would stop early -- check hours_fetched against hours_requested in the manifest before reading the old edge as the retention boundary.

only the contracts actually fetched exist here. Gate lists many USDT perpetuals; a study of BTC alone is not affected, but any cross-asset claim needs the other contracts pulled first, and the rolling window means they must be pulled before they age out.
